961.quote_or_event: When the Mughal emperor Jahangir ordered Guru Arjan to remove supposedly offensive passages from the Adi Granth, the Guru refused and was tortured to death at Lahore in 1606, becoming the first Sikh martyr.
961.explanation: Guru Arjan could have saved his life by altering the scripture he had compiled, but he would not buy his survival at that price.
961.tie_back: The Kural says to give up even what seems indispensable, life itself included, if keeping it would lower one's honour; Guru Arjan gave up his life rather than corrupt the Guru's word.
961._accuracy_note: A strong fit on refusing what life seems to require when the price is dishonour; Sikh tradition frames it as fidelity to God's will and the Guru's word rather than personal or family honour.

962.quote_or_event: “with a good name and reputation, with praise and fame throughout the world- still, if the Lord does not bless you with His Glance of Grace, then who cares? What is the use?”
962.explanation: In the seventh pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak says that even worldwide fame is worth nothing without God's grace.
962.tie_back: The Kural says those who want true glory will not do unworthy deeds even for fame; Guru Nanak likewise puts fame below something higher.
962.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib (pauri 7), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
962._accuracy_note: Next-best: both refuse to treat fame as the highest good, but Guru Nanak measures it against divine grace, not against nobility of conduct, and does not speak of unworthy deeds.

963.quote_or_event: “That man, who in the midst of pain, does not feel pain, who is not affected by pleasure, affection or fear, and who looks alike upon gold and dust;”
963.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who stays the same in pain and pleasure and sees gold and dust alike.
963.tie_back: The Kural asks for humility in prosperity and an upright head in want; Guru Tegh Bahadur asks that neither fortune nor misfortune change who one is.
963.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
963._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Gurbani counsels equanimity across fortune, whereas the Kural prescribes a deliberate counter-posture, bending when rich and standing tall when poor.

964.quote_or_event: “One who has the pride of power within, shall dwell in hell, and become a dog.”
964.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan warns that pride in rule and power ends in degradation, pictured as falling to the state of a dog.
964.tie_back: The Kural says people who fall from their honourable place become as worthless as hair fallen from the head; Guru Arjan likewise pictures the proud as brought down to the lowest state.
964.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
964._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both use a vivid image of debasement after a fall, but Gurbani blames ego and pride in power, while the Kural blames sinking below one's own dignity.

965.quote_or_event: “O Kabeer, the gate of liberation is narrow, less than one-tenth of a mustard seed. The mind has become as big as an elephant; how can it pass through this gate?”
965.explanation: A salok in Guru Amar Das's Gujri ki Vaar, opening with Kabir's name, contrasts a gate smaller than a mustard seed with a mind swollen to the size of an elephant by ego.
965.tie_back: The Kural sets a mountain against a tiny kunri seed to show that the smallest debasing act brings the great low; this verse sets the tiny seed against the huge elephant to show how bulk of self blocks the way.
965.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 509, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, salok (attributed to Kabir, in the Vaar of Guru Amar Das) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
965._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the great-against-tiny imagery is shared, but the lesson differs, since the verse is about ego blocking liberation rather than a small fault ruining a great reputation.

966.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
966.explanation: In his saloks, Guru Tegh Bahadur defines the wise person as one who neither intimidates others nor bows to anyone out of fear.
966.tie_back: The Kural scorns those who trail after people who despise them; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal neither fears nor fawns on anyone.
966.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahala 9 (salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
966._accuracy_note: Next-best: the fearless, unservile person is the opposite of the Kural's fawner, but the verse does not mention scorn, fame or heaven, which the Kural's argument rests on.

967.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
967.explanation: Bhagat Kabir describes the true hero as one who would be cut to pieces rather than leave the field, which Sikh tradition reads as standing firm for righteousness and the weak.
967.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to be called ruined than to live by trailing after one's foes; Kabir's hero chooses to be cut down rather than give ground.
967.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maru, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
967._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on preferring ruin to submission; translations of 'deen' differ (Sant Singh Khalsa 'religion', BaniDB 'those in need'), and the verse is about holding firm rather than refusing to serve one's enemies.

968.quote_or_event: “Death would not be called bad, O people, if one knew how to truly die.”
968.explanation: In the Alahaniyan, songs of mourning in Raag Vadhans, Guru Nanak says death is not to be feared by one who knows how to die rightly.
968.tie_back: The Kural asks whether a life that only keeps the body going can be a medicine against death; Guru Nanak also refuses to treat mere survival as the highest good, since what matters is dying rightly.
968.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahaniyan, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
968._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both reject clinging to bodily life, but for Guru Nanak 'dying rightly' means a life lived in God's Name, not the preservation of personal dignity.

969.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
969.explanation: Guru Nanak says the path of love for God asks for complete readiness to give oneself, pictured as carrying one's own head in hand.
969.tie_back: The Kural speaks of the honourable who would give up life itself rather than live when honour is taken; Guru Nanak asks for the same readiness to give one's life, for love of God.
969.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
969._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse is about surrendering ego and being ready for sacrifice, not about honour; Sikhism forbids taking one's own life, and the yak image has no Sikh parallel.

970.quote_or_event: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, was executed by the Mughal authorities in Delhi in 1675 and is remembered above all for his stand for religious freedom; Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib now stands at the place of his martyrdom.
970.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur chose death over submission to religious coercion, and Sikhs and many others still honour his sacrifice centuries later.
970.tie_back: The Kural says the world forever praises those who would not go on living in disgrace; Guru Tegh Bahadur's memory, kept at Sis Ganj and in Sikh prayer, is exactly such lasting honour.
970._accuracy_note: A strong fit on the lasting reverence earned by refusing dishonour; Sikh tradition sees his death as sacrifice for others' freedom of faith rather than as a matter of personal honour.
